newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Ireland's Robinson closer to UN rights job.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's Robinson closer to UN rights job.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Thursday failed to offer the post of human rights commissioner to Costa Rican envoy Sonia Picado, a clear indication he was leaning toward Irish President Mary Robinson.
Picado, Costa Rica's ambassador to the United States, told reporters after a meeting with Annan that she had been offered alternative jobs related to human rights but would not say what they were.

The two women were the leading candidates for the U.N. human rights commissioner post, based in Geneva. Robinson is backed by the United States and Britain, while Picado is supported by most developing nations.
Annan was expected to announce his decision in July.
Picado, an accomplished attorney and known campaigner for human rights, met Annan on Thursday for the second time this year. Asked if he had offered her the post, she said, "No."
"My highest option would be high commissioner but there are other options the secretary-general also wants me to study," she added.

The post, first suggested nearly 50 years ago, became vacant after Jose Ayala Lasso earlier this year resigned as the first U.N. human rights commissioner to become Ecuador's foreign minister. He was appointed in 1994 for four years.
Robinson, 52, was in New York last Friday and spoke to Annan but revealed little of substance about their talks.
She steps down from her presidency in December after a seven-year term and might have to decide whether she would leave the post earlier.
Annan has been under pressure to appoint a candidate from developing nations for the job and diplomats said he was considering a deputy high commissioner post.
But Picado said she would not take such a job and hinted the two also had spoken of a different coordinating position related to human rights.
Annan has said he wants a human rights component in all U.N. operations from peacekeeping to development and may be considering a coordinator in New York.

"Mrs. Robinson and myself have the highest requirements for the job and there should be a way to coordinate," Picado told reporters. "If you are asking me about a different postion of coordination, I will have to consider it."
But she also said, "If I am not the high commissioner I am not sure that I want to accept another post."
